paragraphs: In the autumn of Long’an’s third year, the first fires at sea appeared beyond the salt flats of Shangyu.

At first there was only one, like a fishing lamp far from shore. An old soldier on night watch studied it from the lookout and told a younger man to steady the sighting pole. Two more lights appeared, then dozens, rising and sinking with the tide. The old soldier’s face changed. There were boats beneath every flame, torches blown almost horizontal by the damp wind yet still burning fiercely red.

Someone began beating a drum offshore, each stroke falling upon the water. A small boat burst from the fog. A white-robed man in a short cloak stood at the bow, a red band around his forehead. The drummer shouted the old cry of the sect, but only the words “new age” reached shore through the wind. The young sentry ran to light the beacon. An arrow struck the wooden post with a sharp thud. He fell into the reeds, and by the time he scrambled out, the foremost boats had grounded on the salt flats. Barefoot men jumped into the water with swords, bamboo spears, hooks, and forks, running toward the government storehouse.

Gu Asheng sheltered his mother behind their grass-thatched shed. His family had boiled salt for three generations, yet not one jar in the house was ever full. The salt they made belonged first to the government. Salt workers received a small monthly food allowance, and in poor years even their fuel was entered as debt. Months earlier his mother had fallen ill with a chill. When he sought medicine on credit, the shopkeeper hesitated half a day before agreeing to deduct it from next year’s salt wages. The debt slip was still tucked beneath a roof beam.

The lock on the official storehouse was smashed. White sacks of salt were piled higher than a man’s shoulder. Someone shouted that each household could take one sack, but nobody dared move first. A young man in white helped an old salt worker to her feet and told her not to kneel; he had only come to open the storehouse. She scarcely heard him and kept crying for the Celestial Master to save her.

The man was Sun En. He corrected her once at first, but by the third time said nothing more. Instead he ordered his followers to bring out the storehouse clerks and inspect the salt ledgers. Workers surged forward, Gu Asheng among them. He took only half a sack, but it pressed painfully against his shoulder. When his mother saw him return, she scolded him for stealing government property and bringing trouble upon them. Then she touched the dry grains of salt and could not bear to withdraw her hand.
“Is it truly ours?” she asked.
Gu Asheng panted. “That is what they say.”
His mother poured the salt into an old clay jar. Halfway through, she stopped. “Asheng, what will you say if the county men come tomorrow?”

He had no answer. Outside, people were laughing louder than the boiling salt vats ever did. He had not heard salt workers laugh like that in years, and he did not want to think further. He helped his mother move the jar beside the stove and set it firmly down.

Three days later Sun En attacked Shangyu. The county had neither reduced the year’s salt levy nor returned the workers’ contracts from the storehouse. Instead its officers meant to investigate every household that had taken salt. Gu Asheng went with Sun En’s men, carrying a scaling ladder. He knew every path across the flats and was thrust to the front to guide them. Arrows rained from the wall. A-Zhou, who the day before had argued with him over a wooden bucket, fell before his eyes with an arrow through his chest. Gu Asheng tried to drag him away but could not lift him, and the advancing men pushed him aside. A-Zhou’s little knife lay in the mud. Gu Asheng picked it up, his hand shaking around the hilt.

Once the city fell, the first doors broken down belonged to the office that collected the salt levy, followed by granaries and tax collectors’ homes. Gu Asheng went to the house of a man who had once pressed his mother to pay her labor debt. The family had fled; he found half a sack of rice and carried it away, intending to go home. At the corner he heard screams. Several recent recruits were dragging off the apothecary’s daughter, accusing her family of transporting salt for the county officials.
Gu Asheng knew the woman. When his mother was ill the year before, it was she who had persuaded her father to let them take medicine on credit.
“She never forced anyone to pay the salt levy!” he cried, standing in their way.

They shouted that he was defending the officials. A punch knocked him down, filling his mouth with blood. He got up and caught hold of the woman’s arm. A man opposite him drew his sword. Just then hooves struck the stone paving. Sun En rode up and ordered the leader of the looters seized and beheaded in the street. At every ward he had wooden signs hung up: Anyone who plunders a private home shall be executed.

Sitting on the wet stones, Gu Asheng watched the culprit led away and felt a small measure of faith. Perhaps the Celestial Master could not only give them salt but stop men from doing evil at will. Yet smoke rose three streets off. A shop by the government offices was burning with townspeople trapped inside. Sun En rode from one place to another, turning corner after corner, but his horse’s hooves could not overtake the cries breaking out everywhere.

The following day Sun En ordered every unit registered. Members of the sect would wear red headbands, and armed men without a recorded name were to surrender their blades. Many who had never joined the faith began searching for red cloth. Gu Asheng cut his mother’s old salt-wrapping cloth into strips and tied one across his forehead.
His mother asked, “Do you believe in him?”
“He gave us salt.”
“Then what is that around your head?”
Gu Asheng considered. “If they recognize me as one of theirs, they won’t keep asking whether I’m a government spy.”

His mother rolled up the remaining red cloth and pressed it beneath the salt jar. She neither urged him to stay home nor judged him. She only told him to knock twice on the wooden frame before coming through the door, so she would know it was her son, not soldiers come to inspect the salt.

More and more people joined Sun En: hill villagers, salt workers, conscripted farmers, and local magnates who arrived with their private followers. Before the altar, white-robed elders promised that the new age would abolish the salt levy, divide land according to the number of people, and recalculate all debts. Beside them, military leaders argued that achievements in battle must first be recorded so rewards could later be distributed by merit. Both promises pleased the crowd. When anyone asked how they would be reconciled, each side said the matter could wait until Kuaiji was taken.

Gu Asheng followed the force through several counties, carrying grain, repairing boats, and guarding crossroads. When he was handed his first heaping bowl of millet, he almost could not bring himself to eat it. He also watched people kill. At first they killed tax collectors; later they killed tenants who refused grain. Men once abused by local strongmen returned with swords for vengeance, often sparing not even the household servants who had labored for their former masters. He saw a youth seize someone by the braid and drag him toward the river. Gu Asheng stood beside the road and, in the end, said nothing.

More than three months later he returned to the Shangyu salt works. The grass shed was empty. A neighbor said government troops had come to reclaim the salt and questioned each household about who had taken any from Sun En’s opened storehouse. His mother would not give them her son’s name. She said she had taken the half sack herself and was taken to the county jail. Gu Asheng went there, but a new seal covered the office gates, and no one knew where the clerks had gone.
“Is my mother still alive?” he asked.

The neighbors dared not answer. One caught his sleeve and begged him to leave quickly. That night he took off his red headband and laid it in his palm, astonished to see how deeply it had cut a mark into his skin. At dawn he tied it on again. The unit checked headbands at every roll call; without one, he would be questioned.

At last Jiankang ordered the Northern Garrison south. By the time Liu Laozhi received the command, the troops at Jingkou had quarreled over their pay several times, and news of Sun En’s rising had reached the various battalions. Some urged them to guard the river mouth first, lest sea raiders attack the capital while the troops were away. But the court pressed urgently: commanderies and counties across Kuaiji were falling, and the foundations of Jin’s rule in the Three Wu lands were in danger.

Liu Laozhi ordered Liu Yu to lead several hundred men in the vanguard. Before leaving camp, Liu Yu told each soldier to carry three days’ dried provisions and leave behind spare sacks. Several veterans laughed at his caution and asked whether he feared the men would fill them with gold and silver. His answer was brief: “People in Kuaiji need rice too. Before you touch a sack, find out whether it was taken from rebels or stolen from a farmer.”

After entering Kuaiji, Liu Yu learned how easy that was to say and how painfully long it took to do. The first village they reached had supplied grain to Sun En’s army. The county commandant demanded that every able-bodied man be chained and taken away. Liu Yu asked how many rebels had arrived; the answer was several thousand. He asked how many households lived in the village; barely two hundred. The commandant declared that anyone refusing grain deserved death. Instead of arguing, Liu Yu had his soldiers fetch the village headman’s granary accounts and casualty rolls, then asked which residents had actually left with weapons. In the end three men confirmed to have joined the rebellion were taken away. The others remained under watch, pending further inquiry.

The commandant stormed off to complain to Liu Laozhi. Two days later Liu Laozhi summoned Liu Yu and berated him for waging war as if conducting trials. Question every village, and the rebels would have fled out to sea. Liu Yu listened standing up. At last he asked if the general would permit the local officials to seize the villagers themselves. Liu Laozhi waved irritably. “Go after Sun En! Stop trying cases for the county magistrates!”

The tide was falling when the armies met by the sea. Sun En’s vessels hurried to escape the shallows, but his rearguard had not boarded. Several bands that answered to different commanders fought each other for the boats. Liu Yu struck across a flank of the mudflats. His infantry waded knee-deep, swords clashing with fish spears in the mud. Seeing people carrying chests and bundles toward the shore, he ordered archers to block the wharf exit while leaving two gaps for those who dropped their weapons to retreat. Some rebels shouted that the Celestial Master had returned to the sea; others cursed the men aboard for deserting their brothers. The sea wind tore red headbands loose and scattered them across the flats.

Gu Asheng could not get onto a boat. He had thrown away his knife and tried to run along the reed roots, but slipped and fell full-length into the mud. Northern Garrison troops hauled him out and tore off his headband. Seeing a wound on his shoulder, one declared that a rebel like him deserved to be cut down on the spot. Gu Asheng insisted that he had killed nobody. Had he followed Sun En? Yes. Had he carried grain for the army? Yes. A sword was about to descend when Liu Yu approached and ordered the prisoner taken aside, his name, home district, and actions to be established first.
“Why did you go with them?”
Gu Asheng’s split lower lip made his words whistle. “Salt.”
“Salt?”
“We boiled salt all year and owed debts into the next. Sun En came and gave my mother half a sack. So I followed him.”
A soldier beside them flared up. “Half a sack of salt was worth rebelling against Jin?”
Gu Asheng looked at the man’s sword for a long time before asking, “Sir, has your household ever spent a whole year unable to eat the salt it boiled with its own hands?”
The soldier cursed, but Liu Yu ordered him silent and asked why Gu Asheng had not gone home afterward. Gu Asheng lowered his head toward a torn strip of red cloth lying in the wet mud.
“Go home, and they question you. Stay with them, and they question you too. After a while, following them was the only way anyone would give me food.”

Liu Yu ordered him recorded as an unverified camp follower and confined separately from those proved to have murdered or plundered. The soldiers protested that everyone could claim never to have drawn a sword. How could they tell truth from lies? Question men from the same unit and village first, Liu Yu said; then check the bodies recovered and the case records. He knew there might not be time, and that some offenders might escape as a result. Still he would not condemn everyone to death on the evidence of a red headband.

Sun En’s boats were already far away. Gu Asheng looked up and watched the foremost white sail disappear into the meeting of cloud and water. Those followers left on the shore were still kneeling and crying that the Celestial Master would come back for them. Gu Asheng did not kneel. He stared at a broken mooring post exposed before the rising tide and remembered the two knocks his mother had forgotten to give the night she was taken from their shed.

A few days later the Northern Garrison began clearing the villages. Identified by people from his home district, with no evidence found that he had killed or plundered, Gu Asheng was released from detention. Yet he still could not return to the salt works. Shangyu officials had come again; anyone recorded as having served with Sun En had to be examined anew. Another salt worker told him his mother had died in the county prison, supposedly of illness. To the end she had insisted she herself took the half sack and that her son had stolen no government salt.

Gu Asheng sat down beneath an embankment after hearing this. At daybreak the water had risen to his shoes before he stood. He made no sound of weeping, but inside his robe he kept a pinch of salt that had become wet, dried again, and hardened into a lump.

The roads south were closed to those fleeing the fighting; more small boats began heading north. Gu Asheng traveled with several salt-working families until they reached a ferry on the Huai. Aboard were wounded men, women, deserters who had taken off their uniforms, and people who still bore the indentation of red cloth across their foreheads. Someone advised Gu Asheng to cover his old wounds before crossing, lest the north-bank officials mistake him for a rebel. He said there was no hiding them and left them uncovered.

A Qin patrol boat stopped the ferry to examine its passengers and collect their weapons. Children disembarked first; the sick were sent to a physician; anyone carrying arms stood in a separate line. A granary clerk asked whether anyone had served under Sun En. Silence fell across the boat. Gu Asheng raised his hand and said that he had.
“Did you kill anyone?”
“No.”
“Can anyone from your unit testify to that?”
“Some are dead. Others are still at sea.”

The clerk turned a page and ordered him sent to the north camp for questioning. Expecting to be bound immediately, Gu Asheng held out his wrists. The military clerk merely told him to surrender the short knife he carried and wrote down his name and native district, then went on to question the next person.

Nearby a woman held a feverish child clutching a strip of old red cloth. When a sentry saw it, he put a hand on his sword. The terrified woman tried to throw the cloth away, but the child clung to it, saying his father had given it to him and that wearing it could save his life. Gu Asheng knew the shade of red. He reached out to shield the child. “Give him water first. It is only a piece of cloth.”

A Qin physician came and carried the child to the medical shelter. The clerk entered the cloth in the evidence register but did not drag away the mother and son. When the woman gave her household details, she asked whether she was now a citizen of Jin or Qin. For the moment, the scribe told her, she would receive a temporary guest registration; if she wanted to return south, the boat register would have to be checked. She understood little and asked only when she could see her boy. The scribe pointed her toward the eastern shelter and told her to go there first.

Trouble broke out on the north bank as well. A group of armed former followers of Sun En had slipped into a refugee camp. At night they killed a camp officer, seized grain, and set fires. Some escaped in the confusion, but flames blocked the main gate. The officer in charge, afraid that rebels would flee among the refugees, delayed opening it. At last a junior commander took an axe to the timber barring a side gate, and hundreds of women and children escaped the flames. The commander was then suspended pending investigation, while the missing attackers continued to roam among the reeds on the riverbank.

An urgent report reached Chang’an, where the ministers argued for half a day. Some wanted every crossing closed; others would bar only able-bodied young men. Fu Rong worried that Longyou had only just been pacified and the commanderies had not rebuilt their forces; they could not afford another camp mutiny at the border. Fu Jian asked whether closing the ferries that night would still allow them to rescue the women and children waiting on the southern bank. The officials of the Department of State Affairs had to concede that a sudden closure would kill more people in the south, while continued admission presented genuine dangers of armed infiltration and disease.

Fu Hong proposed separate camps and registers, with physicians and military clerks forbidden to assume each other’s duties. Every camp would also have an emergency exit that could be pushed open from within during a fire. Those suspected of killing or plundering would be isolated for questioning, without treating everyone on their boat as a rebel. Fu Jian approved a trial in the Huai’s northern districts, with costs and benefits to be reviewed after three months before deciding whether to expand it. The order never used the words “benevolent government.” At its end was one brief note: No guard may seal a life-saving exit on the grounds that spies may be present.

Gu Asheng was questioned three times in the north camp. On the third occasion a scribe complained that the months in his account did not match and ordered him to think again. In frustration Gu Asheng struck the table. “I cannot even find out when my mother was put in prison! How am I supposed to remember which month and day we were marching?”

The scribe stopped writing and watched him for a long while before ordering a separate search of Shangyu’s salt-tax archives. Gu Asheng still could not leave the camp, and no one told him when the case might be resolved. That evening his ration was hot millet gruel with a piece of pickled vegetable so bitterly salty it caught in his throat. Halfway through the meal, he took the hard lump of salt from inside his robe, scraped a tiny grain off with his fingernail, tasted it, and hid it again.

Outside the camp nobody cried out for a new age; no follower of the sect promised that salt levies would vanish forever. Instead, clerks came from shelter to shelter asking how much charcoal and medicine would be needed the next day. Another young clerk posted a notice at the gate explaining where complaints against camp officers withholding rations could be made. Gu Asheng could read only a little. He stood looking at it for a long time, then asked a child who knew his characters to read it aloud. After listening, he carried his empty bowl back inside and thought that one day he might first write to Shangyu and ask where his mother had been buried.
